result.summary: Raises the minimum supported GCC version from 12.1 to 13.1, enforcing support via a CMake check for C++20 `std::format`. It updates CI environments to GCC 13/Ubuntu 24.04, drops active NetBSD cross-compilation from GitHub Actions while updating its environment scripts to GCC 14, and refactors several idioms to use standard C++20 constructs (`std::format`, `std::type_identity`, structured bindings capture in lambdas, and folding expressions).
result.problem: Supporting GCC 12 prevents adopting standard C++20 features such as `std::format`, requires custom workarounds like `ALWAYS_FALSE` for static assertions in dependent contexts, and blocks future transitions toward C++23.
evidence: PR description: 'At some point, it may be fine to drop support for older vanilla systems not shipping with at least GCC 13. (For this bump, only C++20 std::format will become available, but this bump should also pave the way for C++23.)'

Commit messages demonstrate removal of workarounds: 'util: Remove ALWAYS_FALSE type', 'refactor: Use C++20 to capture structured bindings in lambdas', and 'refactor: Use C++20 std::type_identity<T> over std::common_type<T>'.
result.scope_notes: Touches build configuration, CI workflows, and refactors several disparate utility and test files to showcase newly enabled C++ features.
result.changed_since_previous: Added refactors leveraging C++20 and C++17 idioms enabled by the newer compiler minimum: using structured bindings in lambdas, fold expressions in `Vector()`, and `std::type_identity` in place of `std::common_type`.
result.card: PR 36042 raises the minimum supported GCC compiler version from 12.1 to 13.1, validated during CMake configuration with a check for std::format. This enables use of std::format, C++20 structured binding capture in lambdas, std::type_identity, and standard static_assert(false), while laying groundwork for eventual C++23 adoption. CI tasks are updated to Ubuntu 24.04 and GCC 13, and the active NetBSD cross-compile CI job is removed from GitHub Actions due to upstream package availability issues.

risk.why: A mistake in build system compiler checks or CI setup could break builds on supported platforms or exclude downstream packagers unexpectedly.
